name: Próspera

summary.text: Próspera is a privately developed charter city on Roatán, Honduras, created under the 2013 ZEDE law, which allowed semi-autonomous zones with their own legal and regulatory frameworks. Its developer has raised about $120 million, including from venture funds backed by Peter Thiel, Sam Altman and Marc Andreessen, among them Pronomos Capital. After Honduras's Congress repealed the ZEDE law in 2022, the developer brought a CAFTA-DR arbitration claim at ICSID seeking up to $10.775 billion. In September 2024 the Honduran Supreme Court declared the ZEDE framework unconstitutional.

facts.claim: After Honduras's Congress unanimously repealed the ZEDE law in April 2022, Honduras Próspera Inc. and affiliates brought a CAFTA-DR investment arbitration claim against Honduras at ICSID, seeking up to $10.775 billion. ICSID registered it in February 2023 as Case No. ARB/23/2, and it is pending. In October 2025, Honduras's attorney general's office said the claim had been reduced to about $1.63 billion.

facts.claim: On September 20, 2024, the Supreme Court of Honduras ruled by majority vote that the ZEDE law and related constitutional reforms violated unamendable articles of the constitution. A court spokesman said existing zones would be declared illegal, but the court still had to publish guidance on how to handle them.

facts.claim: ICSID Case No. ARB/23/2 was brought by Honduras Próspera Inc., St. John's Bay Development Company LLC and Próspera Arbitration Center LLC against the Republic of Honduras, invoking the ICSID Convention, CAFTA-DR and a Legal Stability and Investor Protection Agreement. The tribunal's procedural history records that the claimants filed their Request for Arbitration on 19 December 2022 (the case tracker gives 20 December), that the ICSID Secretary-General registered it on 3 February 2023, and that the tribunal (Juan Fernández-Armesto, president; David W. Rivkin, appointed by the claimants; Raúl E. Vinuesa) was constituted on 29 January 2024 under CAFTA-DR Article 10.19.

facts.claim: The damages figure originates with the claimants. Their 16 September 2022 notice of intent under CAFTA-DR Article 10.16 stated that damages would be at least several billion US dollars and as high as US$10.775 billion, which they described as an expert firm's valuation of the net present value of their investment plus adjustments. Próspera's 20 December 2022 announcement tied the top figure to a loss of the entire investment. The figure is the claimants' stated claim, not a tribunal finding.
facts.quote: damages would be at least several billion US dollars, and as high as US$ 10.775 billion, which according to the valuation of an expert firm experienced in the quantification of damages in investment treaty arbitrations represents the net present value of Claimants' investment, plus appropriate adjustments.

facts.claim: On 26 February 2025 the tribunal issued its Decision on the Respondent's Preliminary Objections under CAFTA-DR Article 10.20.5, rejecting Honduras's argument that the claimants first had to exhaust local remedies under Decreto 41-88 (its 1988 ICSID implementing law). It held that Decreto 10-2005, which incorporated CAFTA-DR into Honduran law, repealed the exhaustion requirement for the purposes of that treaty, and in the alternative that recourse to Honduran courts would have been futile after the Supreme Court's ZEDE ruling.
facts.quote: the Tribunal has come to the conclusion that Decreto 10-2005, through which Honduras incorporated CAFTA-DR into its legal system, repealed, for the purposes of such Treaty, the Exhaustion Requirement in Decreto 41-88.

facts.claim: The February 2025 decision did not reach the merits of the claims. The case remained active at Procedural Order No. 7 of 6 May 2026, on applications to intervene as amicus curiae, and the U.S. State Department's 2026 Investment Climate Statement for Honduras describes the case as pending. No award or decision on the merits was found in the sources reviewed.

It said damages "will be at least several billion US dollars, and as high as US$10.775 billion if Claimants' entire investment is lost", and that it had tried to avoid filing but the government had refused to cooperate on a negotiated solution.

facts.claim: In a later statement responding to coverage of the reduced figure, Honduras Próspera Inc. said the initial damages estimate in its Request for Arbitration was up to US$10.7 billion in the event of a total loss of the investment; that the primary remedy it now seeks is restitution of its rights under the ZEDE legal framework; and that compensation is sought only as an alternative, presently quantified at US$1.6 billion, which it called highly conservative and subject to change. It cited a Berkeley Research Group valuation putting the intrinsic value of its 30-year business plan at an average of US$10.6 billion, and up to US$26.4 billion, as of 30 September 2025.
facts.quote: compensation is only sought as an alternative, and has presently been quantified in the amount of US$1.6 billion

facts.claim: In written testimony for a 14 July 2026 hearing of the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on Oversight and Intelligence, Erick Brimen, founder and CEO of Próspera, said his company and two American affiliates were in arbitration against the Republic of Honduras at ICSID pursuing a US$1.63 billion indirect-expropriation claim that he described as conservatively valued, and that they had never wanted that fight. He said he founded NeWay Capital in 2013 and moved into Honduras in 2017.

facts.claim: The ZEDE framework rested on a constitutional reform and an Organic Law decree, both approved on 12 June 2013. On 20 April 2022 (some accounts give 21 April) the National Congress voted to abolish the ZEDEs. Because the framework had been written into the constitution, repeal of the constitutional provisions required ratification by the following legislature; the U.S. State Department's 2026 report to Congress says this did not happen, and its 2025 report said the status of the legislation and the repeal was unclear and that Próspera ZEDE continued to operate.
facts.quote: Because the ZEDE law was incorporated into the Honduran constitution, the National Congress needed to ratify the repeal in its subsequent session, which it failed to do.

facts.claim: The U.S. State Department's June 2026 report to Congress on U.S. investment in Próspera ZEDE states that the Honduran Supreme Court's September 2024 decision striking down the ZEDE legal framework applied retroactively to the ZEDEs' inception, and that Próspera and other companies in the zones reportedly continued to operate as before. It says the U.S. government is not aware of any case in which properties in the ZEDEs were determined by a competent tribunal to have been expropriated by the Honduran government, that it generally takes no position on the merits of an investment dispute, and that it has raised the dispute with President Asfura's team since his January 2026 inauguration.
facts.quote: The U.S. government is not aware of any case in which properties in the ZEDEs were determined by a competent tribunal to have been expropriated by the Honduran government.

facts.claim: On 24 February 2024 the World Bank, as depositary of the ICSID Convention, received a written notice of denunciation from the Republic of Honduras. Under Article 71 the denunciation took effect six months later, on 25 August 2024, and the World Bank notified all signatory states. Honduras had signed the Convention on 28 May 1986 and ratified it on 14 February 1989. Article 72 provides that a denunciation does not affect rights or obligations arising from consent to ICSID jurisdiction given before the notice was received; the State Department notes Honduras must still defend the Próspera claim and other previously filed ICSID cases.
facts.quote: On February 24, 2024, the World Bank received a written notice of denunciation of the Convention on the Settlement of Investment Disputes between States and Nationals of Other States (the ICSID Convention) from the Republic of Honduras. [...] the denunciation will take effect six months after the receipt of the Republic of Honduras notice, i.e., on August 25, 2024.

facts.claim: On 6 March 2026 Honduras's newly elected president, Nasry Asfura, signed the ICSID Convention on behalf of Honduras, reversing the 2024 withdrawal; the State Department's June 2026 report said Honduras would rejoin ICSID upon ratification. Arbitration commentary later reported that Honduras deposited its instrument of ratification on 17 July 2026 and that the Convention re-entered into force for Honduras on 16 August 2026, without new legislation removing the exhaustion-of-local-remedies condition in Decree 41-88.
facts.quote: On March 6, 2026, President Nasry Asfura signed the ICSID Convention on behalf of Honduras, reversing the country's 2024 withdrawal.

facts.claim: Honduras's National Congress approved the 2025 General Budget on 5 February 2025 at 430,907.8 million lempiras, which Bloomberg Línea converted to about US$16,903.6 million (EFE: US$16,898.3 million), 5.8% above the 2024 budget. As arithmetic across years (the claim ceiling was stated in 2022), the claimants' original US$10.775 billion ceiling equals about 64% of that one-year budget (10.775 / 16.9), and the US$1.63 billion alternative figure about 10%. Rep. Lloyd Doggett's office described the claim as almost $11 billion, 'nearly two-thirds of the country's national budget', and in other releases as about two-thirds of the 2022 budget.
facts.quote: por monto de 430.907,8 millones de lempiras (HNL), equivalente a unos US$16.903,6 millones, un aumento del 5,8% en comparación al de 2024

facts.claim: On 2 May 2023 Senator Elizabeth Warren and Representative Lloyd Doggett led more than 30 members of Congress in a letter to U.S. Trade Representative Katherine Tai and Secretary of State Antony Blinken asking the administration to intervene on behalf of the government and people of Honduras in the Próspera ISDS claim, including through a statement of support or an amicus brief, and to work to remove ISDS liability from existing agreements in the hemisphere. Reuters reported the letter, citing Próspera's claim of 'at least several billion U.S. dollars and as high as $10.775 billion'. A 2024 letter led by Warren, Whitehouse and Cohen referred back to the May 2023 letter.
facts.quote: urging them to intervene on behalf of the government and people of Honduras in a case brought against it by U.S. company Honduras Próspera under the ISDS system

facts.claim: USTR replied to the May 2023 letter on 25 May 2023 that the President does not believe corporations should receive special tribunals in trade agreements that are not available to other organizations, and that the United States was not pursuing any trade or investment agreements that would establish ISDS. The State Department replied on 26 June 2023 that it was monitoring developments in the Próspera arbitration and noted that CAFTA-DR allows a non-disputing party to make written and oral submissions to an ISDS tribunal on questions of interpretation.
facts.quote: President Biden does not believe corporations should receive special tribunals in trade agreements that are not available to other organizations

openQuestions: Brief claim 'profits are redirected through offshore blind pools into private autonomous jurisdictions such as Próspera': no source reviewed connects revenue from Amazon Web Services, Google Earth or Moderna, or any offshore vehicle, to Próspera's funding. Investors named by sources are Pronomos Capital (its portfolio page), Coinbase Ventures, North Island Ventures and BoostVC (January 2025 announcement), and, per NYT Magazine (2024), venture funds backed by Peter Thiel, Sam Altman and Marc Andreessen. Unsupported as stated.

Brief claim 'backed by Founders Fund': no source reviewed names Founders Fund as an investor in Próspera or in Pronomos Capital. Sources name Peter Thiel personally as Pronomos's anchor or seed investor (Bloomberg Businessweek 2019; Foresight Institute bio) and The Daily Beast names Thiel and Marc Andreessen as Pronomos backers. Founders Fund should not be recorded as a Próspera backer unless a source states it.

Balaji Srinivasan: in this session he is described as a Próspera investor only by secondary blogs (The Dark Atlas, Sovereignty Atlas), which were not cited; a 2022 Metropolis press release names him among Pronomos Capital's backers, and The Daily Beast names him among investors in Praxis. Not recorded as a Próspera connection pending a primary or major-outlet source (Bloomberg Law's 'Libertarian City Dream in Honduras' and Rest of World could not be checked before the search budget ran out).

Brief claim 'legal power to extract sovereign state revenues via supranational tribunals': the record shows a pending ICSID claim, not an award. The 26 February 2025 decision concerned only Honduras's preliminary objections; the latest filing found is Procedural Order No. 7 of 6 May 2026 and the State Department's 2026 Investment Climate Statement calls the case pending. The State Department's June 2026 report says it is not aware of any tribunal determination of expropriation. Enforcement of any future award is not addressed by sources reviewed.

The 'two-thirds of the national budget' comparison mixes years (the US$10.775 billion ceiling was stated in 2022; the sourced budget is the 2025 approved budget of about US$16.9 billion, giving about 64%). Honduras's 2022 and 2023 approved budgets in US dollars were not retrieved; Rep. Doggett's releases variously compare against 'the country's entire 2022 budget' and 'this year'. Against the US$1.63 billion alternative figure Próspera now states, the ratio is about 10%.

Re-accession dates: the 17 July 2026 deposit of ratification and 16 August 2026 entry into force are reported in arbitration commentary (IISD Investment Treaty News, 9 September 2026, or the Kluwer Arbitration Blog 'Honduras Returns to ICSID'); which of the two pages holds those dates was not pinned down. Confirm against ICSID's list of contracting states.

The Supreme Court's September 2024 judgment text and any Honduran gazette publication of the 2022 repeal decree were not retrieved; secondary summaries (Clifford Chance, Latin America Working Group) refer to Decree No. 32-2022 passed on 21 April 2022, while EY gives 20 April. The 2023 constitutional ratification vote did not occur, per the State Department.

Reuters, The New York Times, AP, The Guardian, FT and Wired block the search crawler, so their coverage was not checked in this session. node research/check-links.mjs could not be run in this environment (outbound fetch blocked); the owner should run it before review.
